```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
```

```{r}
# Once again, made-up Nebraska data for this demo. So don't reuse it thinking it's real.
# These are the packages for importing/exporting (rio) and general data work (tidyverse)
pacman::p_load(rio, tidyverse)
```

# Long to wide

```{r}
# Data is read from the R Study Group folder.
# If your EDV drive letter is different than K: you will need to change it.
# NOTE: which = picks the sheet when a workbook has more than one tab. Leave it off and you get the first one.
linelist <- import("K:/R Study Group/Trenton/Ch12 Pivot/pivot_demo_data.xlsx")

head(linelist)
```

```{r}
# Counting up cases one row per LHD and sex.
# This is long data.
counts <- linelist %>%
  count(lhd, sex)

counts
```

```{r}
# names_from is the column/variable whose values we want to turn into the headers
# FYI without values_fill = 0 the empty cells come out NA.
wide <- counts %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = sex, values_from = n, values_fill = 0)

wide
```

# And pivot back to long

```{r}
# cols = -lhd means every column except lhd
# I like to use "-" in some of my work.
# names_to and values_to are just what you want the two new columns called.
# NOTE: 8 rows turn into 16, same numbers just stacked.
wide %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = -lhd, names_to = "sex", values_to = "n")
```

# Why long vs wide? Mostly graphing and Power BI

```{r}
# Plotting package ggplot wants fill= as one column/variable. 
# The wide table has sex split across two.
# You can't do this graph easily in wide but you can with long
# Power BI relies on filters which work with long data.

ggplot(counts, aes(x = n, y = lhd, fill = sex)) +
  geom_col()
```

# Pivoting now by age group

```{r}
# Now counting cases by age group too.
# Count cases then pivot to wide. 
# FYI without values_fill = 0 the empty cells come out NA.

linelist %>%
  count(age_group, sex) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = sex, values_from = n, values_fill = 0)
```
